subject: rla
title: Grammar I: Sentence Structure
objectives: Students will identify complete sentences and correct sentence fragments by adding a missing subject or verb or by attaching a dependent clause or phrase to a nearby sentence.

Students will recognize run-on sentences and comma splices and correct them in five ways: a period, a semicolon, a comma with a coordinating conjunction, a subordinating conjunction, or a semicolon with a transition word.
Students will find and fix misplaced and dangling modifiers so that every describing word or phrase clearly points to the right word.
Students will revise sentences for parallel structure and combine ideas with coordination and subordination that show the correct relationship.
Students will choose transitions that match the logical relationship between ideas, and punctuate them correctly, in GED-style editing items.
teach:
Lesson overview

Week 7 begins the language and editing strand of the GED Reasoning Through Language Arts (RLA) test. On the test, editing questions appear inside short drafts such as workplace emails, notices, and letters. A drop-down menu sits in the middle of a sentence, and the learner chooses the version that makes the sentence correct and clear. This week focuses on sentence structure: whether a group of words is a complete sentence, how sentences are joined, where describing phrases belong, and how ideas are balanced and connected. Week 8 covers agreement, pronouns, tense, confused words, capitalization, and punctuation.

Tell learners they do not need to memorize grammar terms; they need to notice broken sentences and know a few reliable repairs.

Objectives

  • Tell complete sentences from fragments and repair fragments.
  • Identify and fix run-ons and comma splices five ways.
  • Find and fix misplaced and dangling modifiers.
  • Revise for parallel structure; combine ideas with coordination and subordination.
  • Choose and punctuate transitions that match the relationship between ideas.

Materials

  • Student Lesson (printed or on screen) and this week's Notes sheet
  • Whiteboard or shared screen; markers in two colors (one for subjects, one for verbs)
  • Copies of the warm-up list and the guided-practice notice (both below)
  • Index cards with the seven coordinating conjunctions (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) for the support group
  • Week 7 practice items (items 1–6 for independent practice)

60-minute timing plan

SegmentMinutesWhat happens
Warm-up5“Sentence or not?” with six word groups
Direct instruction20Complete sentences; fragments; run-ons and comma splices; coordination and subordination; transitions; modifiers; parallelism; worked examples
Guided practice15Whole-group edit of a six-sentence volunteer notice
Independent practice15Practice items 1–6; circulate and coach
Wrap-up5Checks for understanding; exit ticket; assign the week's study plan

Warm-up (5 minutes): Sentence or not?

Display the list. Learners mark each one S (complete sentence) or F (fragment) and be ready to explain.

  1. When the bus finally arrived.
  2. Stop.
  3. The manager who hired me last spring.
  4. Sign the form and return it by Friday.
  5. Working two jobs and still finding time to study.
  6. I called the office, nobody answered.

Answers: (1) F: “When” makes it a dependent clause; it leaves the reader asking “What happened?” (2) S: the subject you is understood in a command. (3) F: there is a subject (the manager) but no main verb; “hired” belongs to the “who” clause. (4) S: a command with two verbs. (5) F: -ing words alone cannot be the main verb. (6) Trick question: it contains two complete thoughts, but they are joined with only a comma. That is a comma splice, today's second big topic. Length does not decide it: “Stop.” is a sentence; item 5 is not.

Direct instruction (20 minutes)

Talking point 1: What makes a complete sentence (3 minutes)

Say: “A complete sentence needs three things: a subject (who or what), a verb (what the subject does or is), and a complete thought.” A group of words with a subject and verb is a clause. An independent clause can stand alone. A dependent clause starts with a word like because, although, when, if, since, unless, while, which, or who, and it cannot stand alone. Give the test: read the words alone, out loud, as if you just walked into the room. If the listener would say “...and?”, it is not complete.

Talking point 2: Fragments and how to fix them (3 minutes)

Name the three common fragment types: (1) a dependent clause standing alone (Because the system was down.); (2) a phrase with no subject or no main verb (Including all part-time staff. / The new hire from the Tampa office.); (3) an -ing or to phrase (Hoping to finish by noon.). The usual repair on the GED is to attach the fragment to the sentence next to it. The other repair is to add what is missing.

Worked example 1: Fragment

Draft: We are closing early on Friday. Because the electricians need to replace the main panel.

Step 1: Test the second group alone. “Because the electricians need to replace the main panel” leaves the reader asking “...and?” It is a dependent clause.

Step 2: Find the sentence it belongs to. It explains why the office is closing early.

Step 3: Attach it. We are closing early on Friday because the electricians need to replace the main panel. No comma is needed when the because clause comes second. If you move it to the front, add a comma: Because the electricians need to replace the main panel, we are closing early on Friday.

Talking point 3: Run-ons and comma splices (4 minutes)

A run-on (also called a fused sentence) jams two independent clauses together with no punctuation. A comma splice joins them with only a comma. Both are errors because a comma alone is not strong enough to hold two sentences together. Teach the five repairs and write them on the board as a menu.

Worked example 2: Five ways to fix a comma splice

Draft: The printer is jammed, the reports will be late.

Step 1: Check each side. “The printer is jammed” can stand alone. “The reports will be late” can stand alone. Two independent clauses with only a comma: comma splice.

Step 2: Decide the relationship. The jam causes the delay.

Step 3: Choose a repair.

  1. Period: The printer is jammed. The reports will be late.
  2. Comma + coordinating conjunction: The printer is jammed, so the reports will be late.
  3. Semicolon: The printer is jammed; the reports will be late.
  4. Semicolon + transition + comma: The printer is jammed; as a result, the reports will be late.
  5. Subordinating conjunction: Because the printer is jammed, the reports will be late.

Step 4: Point out the trap: The printer is jammed, therefore, the reports will be late. is still a comma splice. Words like however, therefore, also, and then are not conjunctions; they cannot join sentences with a comma.

Talking point 4: Coordination, subordination, and transitions (4 minutes)

Coordination joins equal ideas with a comma and one of the seven coordinating conjunctions: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so (FANBOYS). Subordination makes one idea depend on the other with a word that shows the relationship: because, since (cause); although, even though, while (contrast); when, after, before, once, until (time); if, unless (condition). Transitions such as however, therefore, for example, in addition, and as a result connect sentences. Stress that GED transition questions are really logic questions: read the sentence before and the sentence after, name the relationship (adding, contrasting, cause and effect, example, time), and only then look at the choices.

Worked example 3: Choosing a transition

Draft: The clinic extended its evening hours. [Choose], patients can now book appointments until 8:00 p.m. Choices: However / As a result / For example / Instead

Step 1: Name the relationship. Longer hours cause later appointments to be possible. This is cause and effect.

Step 2: Sort the choices. However and Instead show contrast. For example introduces an example of a general statement. As a result shows effect.

Step 3: Answer: As a result. Check by reading the full pair aloud.

Talking point 5: Misplaced and dangling modifiers (3 minutes)

A modifier is a word or phrase that describes. Rule: put it right next to the word it describes. A misplaced modifier sits next to the wrong word (She served sandwiches to the children on paper plates. The children are not on the plates). A dangling modifier, usually an opening -ing or to phrase, has no correct word to describe in the sentence. The word right after the comma must be the one doing the action.

Worked example 4: Dangling modifier

Draft: After reviewing your application, you have been selected for an interview.

Step 1: Ask who did the action in the opening phrase. Who reviewed the application? The company did, not the applicant.

Step 2: Look at the word right after the comma: you. The sentence says the applicant reviewed his or her own application. That is the error.

Step 3: Fix by putting the doer right after the comma, or by giving the phrase its own subject: After reviewing your application, we have selected you for an interview. or After we reviewed your application, you were selected for an interview.

Talking point 6: Parallelism (3 minutes)

Items in a list or pair must have the same grammatical form: all -ing words, all to verbs, all nouns, or all clauses. Pairs joined by both...and, either...or, not only...but also follow the same rule.

Worked example 5: Parallelism

Draft: The job requires lifting boxes, to drive a forklift, and good communication skills.

Step 1: Underline the list items: lifting boxes (-ing), to drive a forklift (to verb), good communication skills (noun phrase). Three different forms.

Step 2: Pick one form and match the others to it. The job requires lifting boxes, driving a forklift, and communicating clearly.

Step 3: Read it aloud; a parallel list has a steady rhythm.

Guided practice (15 minutes)

Display this draft notice. Each sentence after the first has one error. Learners name the error type first, then the class agrees on a repair.

(1) The Northside Food Pantry needs volunteers for its Saturday distribution. (2) Which runs from 9:00 a.m. to noon. (3) Volunteers sort donations, pack boxes, and they carry groceries to cars. (4) The work is not hard, you should wear closed-toe shoes. (5) Arriving late, the doors will be locked for safety. (6) Shifts fill quickly. For example, sign up at least one week ahead.

Answers:

  • (2) Fragment (dependent clause). Attach: ...for its Saturday distribution, which runs from 9:00 a.m. to noon.
  • (3) Faulty parallelism. Volunteers sort donations, pack boxes, and carry groceries to cars.
  • (4) Comma splice, and the ideas contrast. The work is not hard, but you should wear closed-toe shoes. (A semicolon also fixes the splice, but but shows the contrast better.)
  • (5) Dangling modifier: the doors are not arriving late. If you arrive late, you will find the doors locked for safety.
  • (6) Wrong transition. Signing up early is not an example of shifts filling quickly; it is what to do because of it. Shifts fill quickly, so sign up at least one week ahead. or Shifts fill quickly; therefore, sign up at least one week ahead.

Independent practice (15 minutes)

Learners complete practice items 1–6. Circulate. When a learner is stuck on a drop-down item, ask: “Read the whole sentence with each choice. Which one could you read aloud at work without anyone stopping you?” Items 7–12 are assigned for the week.

Checks for understanding

  • “Is Although the store opens at nine. a sentence?” Expected: No. Although makes it dependent.
  • “Why is I finished early, however, I stayed late. wrong?” Expected: however cannot join two sentences with commas; use ; however, or a period.
  • “What is the first thing to check after an opening -ing phrase?” Expected: the word right after the comma must be the one doing the action.
  • “Name two transitions that show contrast and two that show result.” Expected: however, nevertheless, on the other hand, instead; therefore, as a result, consequently, so.

Common mistakes and how to correct them

  • “Long means run-on.” Learners chop up long, correct sentences. Correct it: a run-on is about structure, not length. Have them find the subjects and verbs.
  • Treating however like but. Correct it with the rule card: FANBOYS can follow a comma; however, therefore, and for example need a semicolon or a period before them.
  • Fixing a splice with the wrong conjunction. The store was busy, so we closed early is punctuated correctly but may say the wrong thing. Always check the logic.
  • Assuming the first sentence of a fragment pair is the problem. Test each group of words alone.
  • Moving the comma instead of the modifier. Adding or removing a comma does not fix a dangling modifier; the right doer must come after the phrase.

Differentiation

Support: Give learners the FANBOYS cards and a two-color routine: circle subjects in one color, underline verbs in another, then count the clauses. Let them fix comma splices only with a period first, then add one new repair at a time. Pair them for the guided practice.

Stretch: Have learners take one comma splice and write all five repairs, then explain how the meaning shifts with so, but, and although. Ask them to write a five-sentence workplace email with three planted errors for a partner to find.

How this shows up on the GED

Language items appear as drop-down menus inside short drafts: emails, memos, notices, letters, and brief articles. A menu may replace one word, a punctuation mark plus the next word, or a whole sentence. Typical forms:

  • A junction between two clauses with choices such as , they / ; they / , They / they. The choices may differ only by a punctuation mark or a capital letter, so learners must read slowly.
  • A transition at the start of a sentence: However, / Therefore, / For example, / In addition,
  • A whole sentence in four versions, only one with the modifier in the right place or the list in parallel form.
  • A subordinating word: Although / Because / Unless / When.

Some practice tests also ask which sentence in a paragraph is a fragment or which revision combines two sentences best. Remind learners to read the entire sentence, and often the sentence before it, with their choice in place before moving on.

Wrap-up (5 minutes)

Run the checks for understanding, give the exit ticket from the Post Lesson, and preview the study plan, including this week's Practice GED.
student:
Why sentence structure matters

On the GED Reasoning Through Language Arts test, some questions show you a draft, such as an email, a notice, or a letter, with drop-down menus in the middle of sentences. Your job is to choose the version that makes the sentence correct and clear. Many of these questions test sentence structure: whether a sentence is complete, how two ideas are joined, where describing words belong, and how lists and ideas connect. The same skills will make your own writing, including your GED essay, clearer.

What makes a complete sentence

A complete sentence has a subject (who or what), a verb (the action or state), and a complete thought.

A group of words with a subject and a verb is a clause. An independent clause can stand alone as a sentence. A dependent clause starts with a word such as because, although, when, if, since, unless, while, which, or who. It cannot stand alone.

Quick test: Read the words alone, out loud. If a listener would ask “...and?” or “...what about it?”, the thought is not complete. Length does not matter. “Stop.” is a sentence. “The new manager from the downtown office” is not.

Fragments

A fragment is a piece of a sentence punctuated as if it were whole. Watch for three kinds:

  • A dependent clause alone: Because the elevator is broken.
  • A phrase with no subject or no main verb: Including all weekend staff.
  • An -ing or to phrase alone: Hoping to finish before noon.

Fix: attach the fragment to the sentence next to it, or add the missing subject or verb.

Example 1

Draft: Our office will be closed Thursday. Because the carpets are being replaced.

Step 1: “Because the carpets are being replaced” is a dependent clause. It cannot stand alone.

Step 2: It explains why the office will be closed, so attach it: Our office will be closed Thursday because the carpets are being replaced.

Run-ons and comma splices

A run-on joins two independent clauses with no punctuation: The store opens at nine it closes at six. A comma splice joins them with only a comma: The store opens at nine, it closes at six. Both are errors. Here are five ways to fix them:

RepairExample
PeriodThe store opens at nine. It closes at six.
SemicolonThe store opens at nine; it closes at six.
Comma + FANBOYS (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so)The store opens at nine, and it closes at six.
Semicolon + transition + commaThe store opens late; however, it stays open until ten.
Subordinating wordAlthough the store opens late, it stays open until ten.

Watch out: however, therefore, also, then, and for example are not joining words. It rained, however, the game went on. is still a comma splice. Write It rained; however, the game went on. or It rained. However, the game went on.

Example 2

Draft: My shift ended at five, I stayed to help close the register.

Step 1: Both sides can stand alone, and only a comma joins them. Comma splice.

Step 2: The ideas contrast (the shift ended, but the writer stayed), so choose a contrast word: My shift ended at five, but I stayed to help close the register. Also correct: Although my shift ended at five, I stayed to help close the register.

Coordination, subordination, and transitions

Choose a joining word that shows how the ideas are related.

RelationshipJoining wordsTransitions
Addingandin addition, also, furthermore
Contrastbut, yet, although, even though, whilehowever, nevertheless, on the other hand, instead
Cause and effectso, because, sincetherefore, as a result, consequently
Example(none)for example, for instance
Timewhen, after, before, once, untilthen, next, afterward, finally
Conditionif, unlessotherwise

Strategy for transition questions: Cover the choices. Read the sentence before and the sentence after. Name the relationship in one word, such as contrast or result. Then pick the choice that matches.

Misplaced and dangling modifiers

A modifier describes something. Put it right next to the word it describes.

  • Misplaced: The customer returned the blender to the store that was broken. (Was the store broken?) Fix: The customer returned the broken blender to the store.
  • Dangling: Running to catch the bus, my phone fell in a puddle. (The phone was not running.) Fix: Running to catch the bus, I dropped my phone in a puddle.

Example 3

Draft: To apply for the job, a resume must be uploaded by Friday.

Step 1: Who is applying? A person. Who comes right after the comma? “a resume.” A resume cannot apply for a job. Dangling modifier.

Step 2: Put the person after the comma: To apply for the job, you must upload a resume by Friday.

Parallel structure

Items in a list or pair must have the same form.

Example 4

Draft: Before the interview, review the job posting, practicing your answers, and you should choose your outfit.

Step 1: List the items: review (command), practicing (-ing), you should choose (full clause). They do not match.

Step 2: Match them to the first: Before the interview, review the job posting, practice your answers, and choose your outfit.

Try it

1. Fix the fragment: Our office will be closed Monday. In honor of Memorial Day.

Show answer

Attach the phrase: Our office will be closed Monday in honor of Memorial Day. “In honor of Memorial Day” has no subject or verb.

2. Fix the comma splice: Rent is due on the first, a late fee is added after the fifth.

Show answer

Any of these: Rent is due on the first. A late fee is added after the fifth. / Rent is due on the first; a late fee is added after the fifth. / Rent is due on the first, and a late fee is added after the fifth.

3. Fix the modifier: Freshly washed and folded, Rosa put the towels in the closet.

Show answer

The towels, not Rosa, are washed and folded. Rosa put the freshly washed and folded towels in the closet.

4. Make it parallel: The class teaches budgeting, how to save, and investing.

Show answer

The class teaches budgeting, saving, and investing. All three are now -ing words.

5. Choose the transition: The new schedule saves the company money. [However / For example / As a result], some employees dislike the early start.

Show answer

However. The second sentence presents a drawback that contrasts with the benefit in the first.

How to approach a GED editing item

  1. Read the whole sentence, and the one before it, before opening the menu.
  2. Try each choice in the sentence. Read it silently as if out loud.
  3. Look closely: some choices differ by only a comma, a semicolon, or a capital letter.
  4. Ask: Is it a complete sentence? Are two sentences joined correctly? Does each modifier point to the right word? Do the list items match? Does the transition make sense?
post:
Summary of key points

  • A complete sentence has a subject, a verb, and a complete thought. Length does not decide it.
  • A fragment is usually fixed by attaching it to the sentence next to it.
  • Run-ons and comma splices join two sentences incorrectly. Fix them with a period, a semicolon, a comma plus FANBOYS, a semicolon plus a transition and comma, or a subordinating word.
  • However, therefore, and for example cannot join sentences with a comma.
  • Put every modifier next to the word it describes. After an opening phrase, the word right after the comma must be the one doing the action.
  • Keep lists and pairs parallel: same form for every item.
  • Pick joining words and transitions by logic first: adding, contrast, cause and effect, example, time, or condition.

Exit ticket

1. What three things does every complete sentence need?

Show answer

A subject, a verb, and a complete thought.

2. Fix this sentence: I finished the report, I emailed it to my manager.

Show answer

Examples: I finished the report, and I emailed it to my manager. / After I finished the report, I emailed it to my manager. / I finished the report; I emailed it to my manager.

3. Which word makes this a fragment: Although the store opens at nine.

Show answer

Although. It turns the clause into a dependent clause. Removing it, or adding a main clause (Although the store opens at nine, the staff arrives at eight.), fixes it.

4. What is wrong with Hanging in the closet, Marta found her uniform.?

Show answer

The modifier points to Marta, so the sentence says Marta was hanging in the closet. Fix: Marta found her uniform hanging in the closet.

5. Choose the best transition: The shop's sales doubled. [For example / As a result / However], it hired two more workers.

Show answer

As a result. Hiring more workers is an effect of higher sales.

Reflection

  • Which error do you make most often in your own writing: fragments, comma splices, modifiers, or lists that do not match? How will you check for it?
  • Which of the five comma splice repairs feels most natural to you? Which one do you want to practice?
  • Look at a text or email you sent this week. Can you find one sentence you would now revise?

This week's study plan

DayWhat to doTime
Day 1Reread the Student Lesson. Redo the Try it problems without looking at the answers.25 min
Day 2Study the vocabulary and the Notes sheet. Write one comma splice and fix it all five ways.25 min
Day 3Complete practice items 1–6. Read every explanation, even for items you got right.30 min
Day 4Complete practice items 7–12. For each miss, name the error type you overlooked.30 min
Day 5Editing drill: write a short email to an imaginary coworker with three planted errors (a fragment, a comma splice, a dangling modifier). The next day, find and fix them.25 min
Day 6Take this week's Practice GED for Reasoning Through Language Arts under timed conditions.40 min, continue on Day 7 if needed
Day 7Finish the Practice GED if needed. Review every missed language item and list the rules to review.30 min

Test-taking strategy: Read the whole sentence with each choice

Drop-down choices are built to look almost the same. One may have a comma where another has a semicolon, or a capital letter where another has a lowercase one. Do not choose from the menu alone. Put each choice into the sentence and read from the beginning of the sentence to the end. Then ask two questions: “Is this correct?” and “Does it say what the writer means?” The right answer passes both tests.

vocab.def: A group of words with a subject and a verb that expresses a complete thought and can stand alone as a sentence.
A group of words with a subject and a verb that cannot stand alone because it begins with a word such as because, although, when, or which.
vocab.example: because the meeting starts at noon

vocab.def: A piece of a sentence written as if it were complete; it is missing a subject, a verb, or a complete thought.
Two or more independent clauses joined with no punctuation or joining word.
vocab.example: The bus was late I missed my class.

vocab.def: Two independent clauses joined with only a comma.
vocab.example: The bus was late, I missed my class.

vocab.def: One of seven words that join equal ideas: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so (FANBOYS). Use a comma before it when it joins two sentences.
vocab.example: The bus was late, so I missed my class.

vocab.def: A word that makes a clause dependent and shows its relationship to the main idea, such as because, although, when, if, or unless.
vocab.example: Because the bus was late, I missed my class.

vocab.def: Joining two ideas of equal importance, usually with a comma and a coordinating conjunction.
vocab.example: I applied for the job, and I got an interview.

vocab.def: Joining two ideas so that one depends on the other, using a subordinating conjunction to show the relationship.
vocab.example: Although I applied late, I got an interview.

vocab.def: A word or phrase that shows how one idea connects to the next, such as however, therefore, or for example.
vocab.example: Sales rose. As a result, the store hired more staff.

vocab.def: A word or phrase that describes another word in the sentence.
vocab.example: In the cracked window, cracked is a modifier.

vocab.def: A describing word or phrase placed next to the wrong word, so the sentence says something unintended.
vocab.example: She served sandwiches to the children on paper plates.

vocab.def: An opening describing phrase with no correct word in the sentence for it to describe.
vocab.example: Walking into the room, the lights went out.

vocab.def: Using the same grammatical form for items in a list or pair.
vocab.example: She likes hiking, biking, and swimming.

notes:
Week 7 RLA Study Sheet: Sentence Structure

Complete sentence = 3 parts

  • Subject (who or what)
  • Verb (action or state)
  • Complete thought (no “...and?”)

Fragments

  • Dependent clause alone: Because it rained.
  • No subject or verb: Including all staff.
  • -ing or to phrase alone: Hoping to win.
  • Fix: attach to the next sentence or add what is missing.

Modifiers

  • Put the modifier next to the word it describes.
  • After an opening phrase, the word after the comma must be the doer.
  • Moving a comma does not fix a modifier.

Parallelism

  • Same form in lists and pairs: reading, writing, and speaking
  • Check pairs: both...and, either...or, not only...but also

Five fixes for run-ons and comma splices

  1. Period: It rained. We stayed in.
  2. Semicolon: It rained; we stayed in.
  3. Comma + FANBOYS: It rained, so we stayed in.
  4. Semicolon + transition + comma: It rained; therefore, we stayed in.
  5. Subordinating word: Because it rained, we stayed in.

It rained, however, we went out. is still a comma splice.

FANBOYS

for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so

Transitions and joining words by relationship

RelationshipJoining wordsTransitions
Addingandin addition, also, furthermore
Contrastbut, yet, although, whilehowever, nevertheless, instead
Cause/effectso, because, sincetherefore, as a result, consequently
Examplefor example, for instance
Timewhen, after, before, oncethen, next, finally
Conditionif, unlessotherwise

Drop-down routine: Read the whole sentence and the one before it. Try every choice in place. Watch commas, semicolons, and capital letters. Check grammar first, then meaning.

stimuli.title: Draft Email: Forklift Safety Training
stimuli.html:
To: All Warehouse Staff
From: Marcus Bell, Warehouse Operations Manager
Subject: New forklift safety training

(1) Starting the week of May 5, every employee who operates a forklift must complete a new safety training course. (2) Because the company is replacing all six of our older forklifts with electric models. (3) The electric forklifts are quieter and easier to steer, they also stop faster and handle differently with a full load.

(4) Each course will be taught by an instructor from the manufacturer. (5) The instructor will cover battery charging, daily inspections, and safe loading. (6) We will hand out a pocket guide to every operator printed on waterproof paper.

(7) Classes will be held on Tuesday and Thursday mornings in the training room. (8) Please sign up by April 25 using the sheet in the break room. (9) Employees who have not completed the course will not be allowed to operate the new forklifts. (10) Thank you for helping keep our warehouse safe.

stimuli.title: Draft Letter: Request for a Donation
stimuli.html:
Westside Community Garden
March 3

Ms. Grace Okafor, Store Manager
Harmon Hardware

Dear Ms. Okafor:

(1) I am writing on behalf of the Westside Community Garden to ask whether Harmon Hardware would consider donating supplies for our spring planting day. (2) Our garden has grown from twelve plots to forty in three years. (3) Families use the plots to grow vegetables, to teach their children about plants, and for meeting their neighbors.

(4) Walking through the garden last fall, the broken fence and cracked hoses were hard to miss. (5) Several plots are in a low corner of the lot. (6) They flooded after every heavy rain last year. (7) This spring, our volunteers hope to build raised beds for those plots.

(8) We are asking for twenty bags of soil, two rolls of fencing, and ten garden hoses. (9) However, we would be glad to post a sign thanking Harmon Hardware at the garden entrance. (10) Planting day is Saturday, April 12, and we would love for your staff to join us. (11) Thank you for considering our request.

Sincerely,
Luis Ferreira
Volunteer Coordinator

items.prompt: The paragraph below is from a draft notice posted at a community pool. Click the sentence that is a fragment.
spans: The Lakeview Community Pool will open for the summer on Saturday, June 7.
Swim lessons for children and adults will begin the following week.
Registration forms are available at the front desk and on the city website.
Including a new evening class for adults who are learning to swim.
Lifeguards will be on duty during all open swim hours.
items.hint: Read each sentence alone. Which one has no subject and no main verb?
items.explain:
Step 1. Check each sentence for a subject, a verb, and a complete thought.

Step 2. “Including a new evening class for adults who are learning to swim” has no subject and no main verb. Including is an -ing word, which cannot be the main verb by itself. (The words who are learning belong to a describing clause about the adults, not to a main clause.) Read alone, it leaves you asking “...what is including it?” This is the fragment. Correct.

Step 3. Check the others. Each has a subject and a verb: pool will open, lessons will begin, forms are, lifeguards will be. A writer could fix the fragment by attaching it to sentence 2: “Swim lessons for children and adults will begin the following week, including a new evening class for adults who are learning to swim.”

items.prompt: Which revision of sentence 2 corrects the error in the email?
options: This training is required because the company is replacing all six of our older forklifts with electric models.
Because the company is replacing all six of our older forklifts, with electric models.
Because, the company is replacing all six of our older forklifts with electric models.
Because the company, which is replacing all six of our older forklifts with electric models.
items.hint: Read sentence 2 by itself. What word keeps it from being a complete thought?
items.explain:
Step 1. Sentence 2 begins with Because, which makes it a dependent clause. Read alone, it leaves the reader asking “...and so what?” It is a fragment.

Step 2. The fix must add an independent clause. “This training is required because the company is replacing...” adds the main clause This training is required and explains why. Correct.

Step 3. The other choices only move or add commas or add a which clause. Each still begins with Because and has no main clause, so each is still a fragment. A comma never turns a fragment into a sentence.

items.prompt:
Read this draft email. Choose the option that correctly completes each sentence.

To: All Staff, Third Floor
From: Tanya Brooks, Office Coordinator
Subject: Fire drill on Wednesday

Hi everyone,

Our building will hold a fire drill on Wednesday at ten in the morning{{0}} will sound for about two minutes. Please leave your desk right away and walk down the east stairway to the north parking lot{{1}} your supervisor will take attendance. Thank you for taking the drill seriously{{2}} helps us make sure everyone knows the way out.

Tanya
items.hint: For each blank, ask whether the words after it could stand alone as a sentence. If they can, a comma alone is not enough. If they cannot, they must stay attached to the sentence before them.
items.explain:
Blank 1. “Our building will hold a fire drill on Wednesday at ten in the morning” and “the alarm will sound for about two minutes” are both independent clauses. A comma alone creates a comma splice; no punctuation creates a run-on; a capital letter after a comma is wrong. The period with a capital letter makes two correct sentences: . The alarm.

Blank 2. “where your supervisor will take attendance” is a dependent clause; it describes the parking lot. It cannot stand alone, so a period (with or without a capital) would create a fragment, and a semicolon must join two independent clauses. Attach it with a comma: , where.

Blank 3. “it helps us make sure everyone knows the way out” is an independent clause, so “, it” is a comma splice and “ it” is a run-on. “, It” is also a splice, with a wrong capital. A semicolon correctly joins two closely related sentences: ; it.

options: The electric forklifts are quieter and easier to steer, but they also stop faster and handle differently with a full load.
The electric forklifts are quieter and easier to steer they also stop faster and handle differently with a full load.
The electric forklifts are quieter and easier to steer, also they stop faster and handle differently with a full load.
The electric forklifts are quieter and easier to steer, however, they also stop faster and handle differently with a full load.
items.hint: Sentence 3 has two complete thoughts. Which choice joins them with a comma plus one of the seven FANBOYS words?
items.explain:
Step 1. Sentence 3 contains two independent clauses: “The electric forklifts are quieter and easier to steer” and “they also stop faster and handle differently with a full load.” Joined with only a comma, they form a comma splice.

Step 2. A comma plus a coordinating conjunction (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) correctly joins two independent clauses. “..., but they also stop faster...” is correct, and but fits the meaning: the forklifts are easier in some ways, but operators must learn how they handle differently. Correct.

Step 3. Removing the comma creates a run-on. “also” and “however” are not coordinating conjunctions, so a comma before them still leaves a comma splice. However would need a semicolon before it.

items.prompt: Which revision of sentence 6 corrects the error in the email?
options: We will hand out a pocket guide printed on waterproof paper to every operator.
We will hand out to every operator printed on waterproof paper a pocket guide.
Printed on waterproof paper, every operator will receive a pocket guide.
Printed on waterproof paper, we will hand out a pocket guide to every operator.
items.hint: What is actually printed on waterproof paper? Put that phrase right next to that word.
items.explain:
Step 1. In sentence 6, the phrase printed on waterproof paper comes right after every operator, so the sentence says the operators are printed on waterproof paper. This is a misplaced modifier.

Step 2. The guide is what is printed on waterproof paper. Moving the phrase next to pocket guide fixes it: “We will hand out a pocket guide printed on waterproof paper to every operator.” Correct.

Step 3. The second choice still places the phrase right after every operator. The last two choices open with the phrase, so the word after the comma (every operator or we) is what the phrase describes; neither people nor the writers are printed on paper. Those are dangling modifiers.

items.prompt:
Read this draft notice. Choose the option that correctly completes each sentence.

Gym Closing for Repairs

The gym at the Fairview Community Center will close for repairs from July 1 to July 21. The floor is being refinished, and the bleachers are being replaced. {{0}} all basketball and volleyball leagues will play at Fairview Middle School for those three weeks. Open gym hours will be canceled during the repairs. {{1}} the fitness room and the pool will stay open on their regular schedule. {{2}} the gym reopens on July 22, leagues will return to their usual times.
items.hint: For each blank, cover the choices and name the relationship between the sentence before and the sentence with the blank: result, contrast, example, or time.
items.explain:
Blank 1. The gym is closing, so the leagues must move. The move is an effect of the closing. As a result, shows effect. However and In contrast signal an opposite idea, and the leagues moving is not an example of the floor being refinished, so For example is wrong.

Blank 2. The sentence before says something is canceled; this sentence says other spaces stay open. That is a contrast. However, is correct. Similarly would mean the same thing is happening, Therefore means result, and For instance introduces an example.

Blank 3. The leagues return at the time the gym reopens. This is a time relationship, so When is correct. Although and Even though show contrast, which makes no sense here, and Unless would mean the leagues return only if the gym does not reopen.

items.prompt: Which revision of sentence 4 corrects the error in the letter?
options: Walking through the garden last fall, our volunteers could not miss the broken fence and the cracked hoses.
Walking through the garden last fall, it was hard to miss the broken fence and the cracked hoses.
Walking through the garden last fall the broken fence and cracked hoses were hard to miss.
The broken fence and cracked hoses, walking through the garden last fall, were hard to miss.
items.hint: Who was walking through the garden? That word must come right after the comma.
items.explain:
Step 1. Ask who did the action in the opening phrase. People were walking through the garden. In sentence 4, the words right after the comma are the broken fence and cracked hoses, so the sentence says the fence and hoses were walking. This is a dangling modifier.

Step 2. Put the walkers right after the phrase: “Walking through the garden last fall, our volunteers could not miss...” Correct.

Step 3. “it was hard to miss” still has no person to do the walking; it cannot walk. Removing the comma does not change who is walking. Moving the phrase into the middle still attaches it to the fence and hoses.

options: Families use the plots to grow vegetables, teaching their children about plants, and to meet their neighbors.
Families use the plots growing vegetables, to teach their children about plants, and meeting their neighbors.
Families use the plots to grow vegetables, to teach their children about plants, and to meet their neighbors.
Families use the plots to grow vegetables, to teach their children about plants, and meeting their neighbors.
items.hint: Look at the form of each of the three items in the list. Which choice makes all three match?
items.explain:
Step 1. Sentence 3 lists three purposes: to grow vegetables, to teach their children about plants, and for meeting their neighbors. The first two are to + verb; the third is for + -ing. The list is not parallel.

Step 2. Make the third item match the first two: “to grow..., to teach..., and to meet their neighbors.” Correct.

Step 3. Each other choice still mixes to forms with -ing forms. The last choice is the most tempting because it fixes the for, but meeting still does not match to grow and to teach.

items.prompt:
Read this draft cover letter. Choose the option that correctly completes each sentence.

Dear Hiring Manager:

I am applying for the shipping clerk position at Brightline Supply. {{0}} I have not worked in shipping before, I spent four years as a stock clerk at Delgado's Market. In that job, I received deliveries, checked invoices against orders, and {{1}}. My supervisor often asked me to train new employees on the store's inventory scanner.

{{2}} I would welcome the chance to discuss the position with you.

Sincerely,
Keisha Warren

options: Eager to learn new systems, your inventory software is something I could quickly master.
Eager to learn new systems, I am confident that I could quickly master your inventory software.
Eager to learn new systems, my confidence is that I could quickly master your inventory software.
Eager to learn new systems, it would be easy for me to master your inventory software.

items.hint: Blank 1: does the writer's lack of shipping experience cause her stock clerk job, or contrast with it? Blank 2: match the form of received and checked. Blank 3: who is eager to learn?
items.explain:
Blank 1. Not having shipping experience is a weakness; four years as a stock clerk is a related strength. The ideas contrast, so Although is correct. Because and Since would claim her lack of experience caused her to work at the market, and So that shows purpose.

Blank 2. The list is received deliveries, checked invoices..., and ___. The first two items are past-tense verbs, so the third must be too: kept the stockroom organized. The -ing form, the passive clause, and the full clause beginning with I break the parallel pattern.

Blank 3. The opening phrase Eager to learn new systems describes the writer, so I must come right after the comma: Eager to learn new systems, I am confident that I could quickly master your inventory software. In the other choices, the word after the comma is your inventory software, my confidence, or it; none of these can be eager, so each is a dangling modifier.

items.prompt: Which is the best replacement for However, at the beginning of sentence 9?
items.hint: Read sentences 8 and 9 together. What is the garden offering, and why?
items.explain:
Step 1. Name the relationship. Sentence 8 states what the garden is asking for. Sentence 9 states what the garden will give back: a sign thanking the store. That is an exchange, not a contrast, so However is the wrong transition.

Step 2. In return, signals something given back for something received. Correct.

Step 3. On the other hand and Instead both signal contrast or replacement; the sign is not offered in place of the request. For example would mean the sign is an example of the supplies requested, which makes no sense.

items.prompt:
Read this draft memo. Choose the option that correctly completes each sentence. Pay close attention to punctuation and capital letters.

To: All Front Desk Staff
From: Lena Ortiz, Office Manager
Subject: New visitor sign-in procedure

Beginning Monday, every visitor must sign in on the tablet at the front desk{{0}} sign-in sheets will no longer be used. The tablet prints a name badge that each visitor must wear at all times{{1}} anyone who refuses a badge should not be allowed past the lobby. Contractors may enter work areas only with an escort. {{2}} Please contact me with any questions.

options: After signing in, a staff member must walk contractors to the work area.
A staff member must walk contractors to the work area after signing in.
After contractors sign in, a staff member must walk them to the work area.
After signing in, the work area is where a staff member must walk contractors.

items.hint: Blanks 1 and 2 each join two complete sentences. Which punctuation can do that alone, and how is a word like therefore punctuated in the middle of a sentence? For blank 3, ask who signs in.
items.explain:
Blank 1. “every visitor must sign in on the tablet at the front desk” and “paper sign-in sheets will no longer be used” are both independent clauses. A comma alone (with or without a capital) is a comma splice, and no punctuation is a run-on. A semicolon joins two independent clauses, and the word after it stays lowercase: ; paper.

Blank 2. Again two independent clauses are joined, this time with the transition therefore. A transition cannot join clauses with commas alone, so “, therefore,” is a comma splice and “ therefore,” is a run-on. After a semicolon, the next word is not capitalized, so “; Therefore,” is wrong. The correct pattern is semicolon, transition, comma: ; therefore, anyone. The logic also fits: because visitors must wear badges at all times, anyone who refuses one stays in the lobby.

Blank 3. The contractors are the ones who sign in. “After signing in, a staff member...” says the staff member signs in, a dangling modifier. Moving after signing in to the end does not help: the phrase still attaches to the subject, a staff member, so the sentence still says the staff member signs in. In the last choice, the word after the comma is “the work area,” which cannot sign in. Giving the clause its own subject fixes it: After contractors sign in, a staff member must walk them to the work area.

items.prompt: Which is the most effective way to combine sentences 5 and 6?
options: Several plots are in a low corner of the lot, they flooded after every heavy rain last year.
Although several plots are in a low corner of the lot, they flooded after every heavy rain last year.
Several plots flooded after every heavy rain last year because they are in a low corner of the lot.
Unless several plots are in a low corner of the lot, they flooded after every heavy rain last year.
items.hint: Decide how the two ideas are related. Does being in a low corner explain the flooding, contrast with it, or set a condition for it?
items.explain:
Step 1. Find the relationship. Water collects in low spots, so the plots flooded because they sit low. Sentence 5 states the cause; sentence 6 states the effect.

Step 2. The combination must show cause and effect and be punctuated correctly: “Several plots flooded after every heavy rain last year because they are in a low corner of the lot.” Correct. It also leads naturally into sentence 7, which describes the fix.

Step 3. The first choice is a comma splice. Although signals contrast, but flooding is exactly what you would expect in a low spot. Unless sets up a condition that reverses the meaning: it says the plots flooded only if they were not in the low corner.
